# The Patience of Lichens

Somewhere in the Arctic, on a rock that has never had a name, there is a crusty gray-green patch about the size of your hand. It might already have been growing when the Roman Empire fell. It advanced a fraction of a millimeter this year and will advance a fraction of a millimeter next year, and at that pace it could outlast every country currently on the map. You have almost certainly walked past hundreds of its relatives — on gravestones, tree bark, garden walls, roof shingles — without giving one of them a second thought. Almost nobody does. This strikes me as a failure of imagination on our part, and worth correcting.

So what is a lichen? For centuries the answer seemed obvious: a strange little plant, a moss of sorts. It is not a plant, and stranger still, it is not really an organism — not in the way we usually mean. A lichen is a partnership. A fungus, which cannot make its own food but is magnificent at structure, builds a body: layers, threads, a grip on bare stone. Inside it lives an alga or a cyanobacterium, which is a superb cook, turning sunlight into sugar, but too fragile to hold itself together in the open world. The fungus builds the house; the alga pays rent in sugar. Neither is much of anything alone. Together they become something new — a creature that lives on naked rock, eats light, and appears not to know how to die of old age.

When this was proposed in the 1860s by the Swiss botanist Simon Schwendener, lichenologists were not delighted; they were insulted. The idea that their beloved lichens — a pure and unified kingdom, as they saw it — were actually a fungus running a sugar farm was ridiculed for decades. Among the researchers doing early work on the question was Beatrix Potter — yes, that one — who spent the 1890s drawing and studying fungi with real rigor. Her paper was read at the Linnean Society on her behalf, because women couldn't attend the meetings, and then quietly set aside. She went off and wrote the rabbit books instead, which turned out fine for her. But you do wonder what else we didn't get.

What the partnership buys them is range. Lichens live where almost nothing else can. In the dry valleys of Antarctica — the closest thing on Earth to Mars — the vegetation consists almost entirely of them, and some don't bother living on the rock; they live inside it, a faint green shimmer a millimeter beneath the surface, filtering light through the quartz. In 2005 the European Space Agency strapped lichens to the outside of a satellite and left them in open space for two weeks: hard vacuum, cosmic radiation, unfiltered ultraviolet. When they came back down, they resumed photosynthesis as if they'd been kept in a drawer. There are accounts of dried specimens reviving after decades in museum storage. You can desiccate a lichen into what looks like a dead husk, forget about it for ten years, and it will simply get on with things when water returns.

But their real work is slower and larger than survival: lichens build worlds. They are almost always the first ones there — on new lava in Iceland, on rock freshly uncovered by a retreating glacier, on the blast-scarred slopes of Mount St. Helens. They secrete mild acids that etch microscopic pits into bare stone. They trap windblown dust. They die in patches and mix themselves into the mineral grit. Given a few centuries, this becomes the first true soil. Then moss arrives, then grass, then a seed in a bird's droppings, and eventually a forest — all of it standing on ground that a gray crust began making when nothing else could live there. Every cathedral grove is built on the patience of lichens.

Because they take everything directly from the air and rain, with no skin to shed and nowhere to hide, they are honest to a fault about what's in it. Industrial cities once had lichen deserts around them — zones where the air was too poisoned for a single species to survive. When the air began to be cleaned, the lichens moved quietly back in, and ecologists read them like instruments. There is a poem somewhere in the fact that some of our most sensitive environmental monitoring has been performed by patches on tombstones.

And here is the humbling part: after a century and a half of study, we still had them wrong. In 2016, a researcher named Toby Spribille found that many lichens carry a third partner nobody had noticed — a yeast, tucked into the outer layer. Two specimens with identical genomes can look entirely different, one yellow and one brown, because of this hidden resident. The tidy two-organism story became a small ecosystem wearing a single body. We had them under the microscope for 150 years and were missing an entire participant. It suggests a healthy posture going forward: hold your certainties loosely. The world is full of things we are probably flatly misreading right now.

I think about lichens partly because they're astonishing and partly because they argue a philosophy. We're raised on stories of speed: the cheetah's sprint, the falcon's stoop. But nearly all that drama stands on a foundation of slowness. Soil is made by patience — by organisms willing to spend ten thousand years dissolving rock into the mere possibility of a tree. And the method was never conquest; it was collaboration. A fungus and an alga, then a yeast, then the wind, then time. Individually unremarkable, together nearly immortal. That is not a bad account of the only things that have ever really lasted — languages, cathedrals, science, love. Nothing durable was ever built by a single self.

So here is my small proposal. Sometime today you will pass a tree, a wall, or a stone wearing its quiet gray-green crust. Stop for ten seconds. That patch may be older than your grandmother, older than the tree itself, older than the wall it's slowly dissolving. It was photosynthesizing before your country had its name, and it will keep at it long after everyone currently alive is gone — negotiating its ancient deal, trading minerals for sugar, eating light. It doesn't need you to notice it. But noticing it recalibrates something. It reminds you that the world is not only what happens fast, and that some of the most important work being done on Earth at this moment is growing about a millimeter a year.
